extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; early-18th-century literate public (and theatre practitioners/interested managers)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted criteria and prescriptive observations embedded in Addison & Steele's Spectator essays about theatre design/management, criticism, and authorial conduct; aimed at general literate readers and people involved with theatre. Contains historical examples used as informal guidance for producing and evaluating theatrical/published work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre architecture and audibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The house was too large, and its architecture swallowed up the voices of the actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce auditorium dimensions and high ceilings to improve audibility — e.g., they 'contracted the width of the theatre, brought down its enormously high ceiling, thus made the words of the plays audible.' Practical example: modifying physical proportions of the Haymarket improved speech intelligibility and audience reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match repertoire to audience and location
rubrics_metrics.description: Vanbrugh and Congreve opened their grand west-end theatre with concession to the new taste of the fashionable for Italian Opera; they began with a translated opera set to Italian music, which ran only for three nights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose programming that suits the local audience's tastes and accessibility. The Haymarket's initial failure was partly because surrounding fields cut off poorer City playgoers (who couldn't afford coach-hire) and because the programming (Italian opera) did not attract sufficient paying audiences in that location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding and subscription model for theatres
rubrics_metrics.description: Thirty persons of quality having subscribed a hundred pounds each towards the cost of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subscription by patrons of quality to fund theatre construction and operations. Historical example: the Haymarket was financed by subscriptions which reflected the tastes and influence of its backers; subscription models shape repertoire and managerial expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre management: licensing, profit‑sharing and scheduling
rubrics_metrics.description: It was agreed that while 'Drury Lane' confined itself to the acting of plays, he should profit by the new taste for Italian music, and devote the house in the 'Haymarket' to opera... the actors to pay Collier two hundred a year for the use of his license, and to close their house on the Wednesdays when an opera was played.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiate licenses, delineate artistic domains (plays vs. opera), agree profit-sharing, and coordinate schedules to avoid conflicts. Practical management arrangements (swapping licenses, paying for license usage, agreed closed days) can stabilize competing houses and reconcile actor/singer availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a good critic
rubrics_metrics.description: He is an excellent Critick... Aristotle and Longinus are much better understood by him than Littleton or Cooke... His Familiarity with the Customs, Manners, Actions, and Writings of the Antients, makes him a very delicate Observer of what occurs to him in the present World.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good critic is learned (classical knowledge prized), a delicate observer of contemporary manners and performances, attends plays regularly, and offers judgments that actors desire to please. Being well-read and judicious increases a critic's influence on theatrical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial principle: write to satisfy your own mind rather than fame
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an endless and frivolous Pursuit to act by any other Rule than the Care of satisfying our own Minds in what we do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should prioritise internal standards and the design of their work over anxious pursuit of reputation. Be 'very careful of the Design of my Actions, but very negligent of the Consequences of them' — i.e., focus on craft and conscience rather than external approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of silence and observation as a writer's method
rubrics_metrics.description: To be exempt from the Passions with which others are tormented, is the only pleasing Solitude... I have indulged my Silence to such an Extravagance... The working of my own Mind, is the general Entertainment of my Life... Such an Habit has perhaps raised in me uncommon Reflections; but this Effect I cannot communicate but by my Writings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ reserved public behavior and close visual/mental observation as a source of material and insight. Silence and solitude cultivate the faculty of observation and inward reflection that nourish writing; prefer seeing and reflecting over active social engagement when developing ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt style and tone to your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: When it is a Woman's Day, in my Works, I shall endeavour at a Stile and Air suitable to their Understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor the style, tone, and register of a piece to the intended readership (here: women). Explicitly adapt language and approach to suit the audience's presumed understanding and interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value originality; penalise imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Though I allow a Beauty to be as much to be commended for the Elegance of her Dress... if she has stolen the Colour of her Ribbands from another, or had Advice about her Trimmings, I shall not allow her the Praise of Dress, any more than I would call a Plagiary an Author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality is a mark of merit; copying or parroting another's design reduces rightful praise. Apply the same standard to aesthetic and intellectual work — imitation undermines genuine praise and authorship.
